quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: You open the fridge and find your labeled leftovers gone. Your roommate is watching TV in the next room.
quests.correctAnswer: Take a breath, then go ask if they know what happened to your food
quests.hint: Your first thought might be to march in accusing them. What's a calmer opening move?
quests.explanation: Starting with a question instead of an accusation leaves room for an innocent explanation and avoids an unnecessary fight.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: You've had a rough day and just found your headphones tangled in a knot after your younger sibling borrowed them without asking.
quests.correctAnswer: Set them aside and bring it up once you've cooled down
quests.hint: Being extra tired or stressed makes small annoyances feel bigger than they are. What helps you respond fairly?
quests.explanation: Reacting while already stressed often makes a small issue sound bigger than it is; a short delay keeps your response proportional.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: In a group chat, someone replies to your idea with 'that's kind of a dumb plan lol.' You feel your face go hot.
quests.correctAnswer: Wait a few minutes before typing anything back
quests.hint: Firing back the first thing that comes to mind rarely reads well later. What buys you better judgment?
quests.explanation: A short pause before responding to a sharp comment prevents you from escalating a text exchange you can't easily undo.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: A close friend hasn't replied to your texts in two days, even though they were online. You start imagining reasons why they're upset with you.
quests.correctAnswer: Send a direct message asking if everything is okay between you two
quests.hint: You're filling the silence with guesses. What actually gets you an answer?
quests.explanation: Checking directly closes the gap between what you imagine and what's actually true, instead of building a case against your friend in your head.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: Several coworkers went to lunch together and didn't mention it to you. You wonder if you're being deliberately left out.
quests.correctAnswer: Ask a coworker casually whether the lunch was planned last-minute
quests.hint: There are several harmless reasons this could have happened.
quests.explanation: A casual question usually reveals an ordinary explanation, and asking is far less costly than quietly resenting people over an assumption.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: Two classmates start laughing right after you answer a question in class. You immediately assume they're mocking you.
quests.correctAnswer: Ask one of them privately later what was actually funny
quests.hint: Laughter right after you speak feels personal, but it might have nothing to do with you.
quests.explanation: Checking privately, away from the group, lets you get real information without publicly confronting people over something that might be unrelated.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: A classmate next to you keeps clicking their pen during a quiet study session, and you're losing focus.
quests.correctAnswer: Quietly ask them to stop clicking the pen because it's distracting you
quests.hint: The distraction is small but real. What's the most direct, low-drama way to fix it?
quests.explanation: Saying exactly what the behavior is and how it affects you gets it fixed immediately, without a bigger conversation.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: You're telling a friend about your day, but they keep glancing at their phone and scrolling.
quests.correctAnswer: Say lightly, 'Can I have your attention for a second? This actually matters to me.'
quests.hint: You could just stop talking and feel resentful, or you could name what you need. Which helps more?
quests.explanation: Naming what you want in the moment, without accusing them of not caring, gives them an easy way to correct course.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: Your cousin has borrowed your phone charger three times this month and keeps forgetting to give it back.
quests.correctAnswer: Tell them clearly you need it returned the same day each time from now on
quests.hint: A vague 'please give it back sometime' hasn't worked so far. What kind of request actually sticks?
quests.explanation: A specific, repeatable expectation is easier for someone to follow than a general complaint, and it prevents the pattern from continuing.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: Your roommate has a big exam tomorrow and is clearly stressed. You've been meaning to bring up the chore schedule.
quests.correctAnswer: Hold off on the chore conversation until after their exam
quests.hint: The chore issue isn't going anywhere, but their stress level right now might affect how they hear you. What's the better call?
quests.explanation: Raising a manageable issue at a worse moment can turn it into a bigger conflict than it needs to be; timing changes how a message lands.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: You want to ask your parent about weekend plans, but they're in the middle of an urgent-sounding work call.
quests.correctAnswer: Wait until the call ends before bringing it up
quests.hint: Your question isn't urgent, but their call clearly is. What shows basic consideration here?
quests.explanation: Interrupting something time-sensitive for a non-urgent request usually backfires; waiting a few minutes costs you nothing.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: Your friend is venting to you about a rough week. You also have a small complaint about something they did last weekend.
quests.correctAnswer: Save your complaint for a separate, calmer conversation later
quests.hint: Piling your issue onto their bad moment rarely goes well. What's the better sequencing?
quests.explanation: Adding your own grievance while someone is already upset about something else tends to make them feel attacked instead of heard.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: Your sibling shows up 40 minutes late to pick you up. You're annoyed and about to say something sharp.
quests.correctAnswer: Let them explain what happened before reacting
quests.hint: You don't yet know why they're late. What should come before your reaction?
quests.explanation: Hearing the full explanation first means your response actually fits what happened, instead of assuming the worst.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: A teammate starts explaining how a mistake happened in the shared report, but you're tempted to jump in and point out the error yourself.
quests.correctAnswer: Let them finish their explanation before responding
quests.hint: Interrupting to prove the mistake might feel satisfying, but does it help you understand what happened?
quests.explanation: Letting someone finish shows you're trying to understand the situation, not just waiting for your turn to be right.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: A neighbor comes over looking annoyed, saying your car is blocking part of their driveway.
quests.correctAnswer: Listen to their full concern before explaining your side
quests.hint: Your instinct might be to defend yourself immediately. What comes first?
quests.explanation: Hearing someone out fully, even when you disagree, keeps a small disagreement from turning into two people talking over each other.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: Your friend forgot your birthday this year. You're hurt and tempted to say 'you never think about anyone but yourself.'
quests.correctAnswer: Tell them specifically that forgetting your birthday hurt your feelings
quests.hint: There's a difference between naming what happened and attacking who they are. Which one actually gets heard?
quests.explanation: Pointing to the specific incident invites a real conversation, while a sweeping label like 'you never' invites defensiveness instead of listening.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: A teammate messed up one shift at the shared project booth. You're frustrated and thinking of saying they're 'always unreliable.'
quests.correctAnswer: Point out the specific shift that was missed and ask what happened
quests.hint: One missed shift is a fact you can discuss. A permanent label isn't. What keeps this productive?
quests.explanation: Sticking to the specific event keeps the conversation solvable, since a broad accusation makes people defend their character instead of fixing the problem.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: Your relative keeps leaving the porch light on overnight. You're annoyed and want to say they 'never think about the electric bill.'
quests.correctAnswer: Mention the specific habit and ask them to turn it off when they're last inside
quests.hint: You want the light turned off, not an argument about their character. What request gets you there?
quests.explanation: Focusing on the concrete habit, rather than a character judgment, gives the person something actionable to actually change.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: Something in the shared apartment fridge has started to smell, and you suspect it's your roommate's container, but you're not fully sure.
quests.correctAnswer: Leave a friendly note on the fridge
quests.hint: Calling someone out publicly for something you're not certain about risks embarrassing the wrong person. What's a safer approach?
quests.explanation: A general, friendly note fixes the smell without publicly blaming someone who might not even be responsible.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: You disagree with where your friend group wants to go this weekend, and the debate is happening in a group chat with six people.
quests.correctAnswer: Message the friend organizing the plan privately with your preference
quests.hint: A public group chat argument can turn a small preference into a group-wide debate. What's a more contained way to raise it?
quests.explanation: Taking a minor disagreement to a private message avoids putting pressure on everyone in the group chat to pick a side.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: You notice a classmate's shared study notes have a factual error that a few people are already using.
quests.correctAnswer: Message the classmate directly to point out the error before it spreads
quests.hint: Posting the correction publicly could embarrass them in front of everyone. What's a more considerate first step?
quests.explanation: A private correction fixes the mistake just as effectively while giving the person a chance to fix it themselves without public embarrassment.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: A group project teammate keeps submitting their part right at the deadline, leaving no time to review it.
quests.correctAnswer: Ask them to send their part two days before the deadline going forward
quests.hint: Telling them to 'be more responsible' doesn't tell them what to actually do differently.
quests.explanation: A specific, concrete ask is far more likely to change behavior than a vague complaint, because it removes any guesswork.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: Your roommate says they'll 'clean more' after you mention the apartment is messy, but nothing changes over the next week.
quests.correctAnswer: Propose splitting specific chores, like you handle the kitchen and they handle the bathroom
quests.hint: 'Clean more' means something different to each of you.
quests.explanation: A concrete division of tasks removes the guesswork that vague promises leave behind, and makes it easy to notice if something's being skipped.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: A friend is often late to plans, and after you mention it, they just say 'I'll try to be better.'
quests.correctAnswer: Ask them to commit to a specific arrival time, like within ten minutes of the plan
quests.hint: A vague promise to 'try' is hard to hold anyone to.
quests.explanation: A specific, measurable expectation gives both of you a clear standard, instead of a vague intention that's easy to forget.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: Earlier today you snapped at a friend over something minor because you were stressed about an unrelated deadline.
quests.correctAnswer: Apologize specifically for snapping, and explain you were stressed, not blaming them
quests.hint: A vague 'sorry' can feel hollow. What makes an apology actually land?
quests.explanation: Naming exactly what you did wrong shows you understand the impact, which usually repairs the moment faster than a generic apology.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: You forgot to pass along an important message to a teammate, and now they missed a deadline because of it.
quests.correctAnswer: Own the mistake right away and help them figure out how to fix it
quests.hint: It might be tempting to downplay it or explain it away first. What actually helps here?
quests.explanation: Taking responsibility immediately, before offering excuses, keeps the focus on solving the problem instead of managing your own image.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: You misread a short text from a friend as rude and fired back an angry reply, only to realize afterward you'd misunderstood the tone.
quests.correctAnswer: Message them back, admit you misread it, and apologize for the angry reply
quests.hint: The instinct might be to just let it drop and move on. Why isn't that enough here?
quests.explanation: Admitting the misunderstanding directly repairs the specific harm done by your reply, rather than leaving a sour moment hanging.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: A friend uses a phrase that mildly annoys you, but it's the first time you've noticed it and it didn't really affect anything.
quests.correctAnswer: Let it go since it's minor and only happened once
quests.hint: Not every irritation needs a conversation. What tells you this one doesn't?
quests.explanation: Raising every small, one-time annoyance can wear on a friendship faster than the annoyance itself; some things are fine to let pass.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: A coworker uses the last of the stapler pins without asking, which is a trivial inconvenience.
quests.correctAnswer: Let it go and just get more pins later
quests.hint: This costs you almost nothing to fix yourself. Is a conversation really necessary?
quests.explanation: Part of good judgment in conflict is recognizing when something is too minor to be worth anyone's time or attention.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this situation.
quests.scene: Your neighbor's kid accidentally kicks a ball into your yard for the first time and looks a little nervous about it.
quests.correctAnswer: Toss the ball back with a smile and not make it a bigger deal
quests.hint: This was accidental and hasn't happened before. What response fits the situation?
quests.explanation: Matching your response to the actual size of the problem keeps small, harmless moments from turning into unnecessary tension with neighbors.
